questions.q: Why can't a cloud credential be written directly into a pipeline's YAML file?
options: GitHub Actions does not support environment variables
Anyone who can read that file, now or later in its Git history, can read the secret
Pipeline platforms automatically reject any file containing text
YAML files cannot technically contain string values
questions.explain: A secret in a tracked YAML file is exposed the same way a hardcoded secret in application code is — it's readable now and in history later.

questions.q: Where does GitHub Actions store a secret, and how is it used by a workflow?
options: In a public file in the repository root
Under the repository's Settings, injected as an environment variable only while a job is running
Directly inside the workflow YAML file as plain text
It cannot be used by workflows at all, only by local scripts
questions.explain: GitHub Actions secrets are stored separately from the repo's code and injected as environment variables at runtime only.

questions.q: What does a Key Vault–linked variable group in Azure DevOps do differently from a regular variable group?
options: It pulls secret values live from Azure Key Vault instead of the pipeline platform storing its own copy
It stores secrets directly inside the pipeline YAML file
It disables all secret masking in build logs
It requires every secret to be entered manually before each run
questions.explain: Linking a variable group to Key Vault means Azure DevOps pulls the current value each run rather than duplicating a stored copy.

questions.q: In `AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET: ${{ secrets.AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET }}`, when is the real secret value resolved?
options: When the YAML file is first written and saved to the repo
It is resolved by the developer's local machine before committing
It never gets resolved — the expression is just a comment
Only at run time, by the pipeline platform itself
questions.explain: The ${{ secrets.X }} syntax is a placeholder resolved to the actual value only while the job runs, never written into the file.

questions.q: Why is `echo "Connecting with $AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET"` dangerous even if the secret is stored correctly?
options: It can print the secret into the build log, and masking isn't guaranteed once a value is transformed
It has no real effect and is completely safe
It permanently deletes the secret from the secret store
It automatically rotates the credential to a new value
questions.explain: Secret masking can fail to catch a value that's been transformed or embedded in a longer string, so echoing it can still leak it into logs.
